accuracy.evidence: Placement checked against Development Matters 2021, Reception Mathematics, which lists 'count objects, actions and sounds'; the abstraction principle (any collection, including sounds and movements, can be counted) is Gelman and Gallistel 1978. Every count in the lab checked by hand: drum rounds 3 and 5, frog targets 4 and 6 with too-many and too-few refused, pair 1 is 3 loud vs 3 quiet (same), pair 2 is 2 giant stamps vs 4 mouse taps (mouse more), bell 5 rings = 5 fingers, robot 1,2,3 for 3 claps (right), 1-5 for 4 claps (extra), 1-4 for 3 claps with one big (big counted twice), 1-4 for 5 claps (missed a quick one), 1,2 for 2 jumps (right). Parameterised answers a and a+b stay 2 to 6 at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips with sounds and actions (Fuson 1988 on keeping track; Gelman and Gallistel 1978): only touchable things can be counted (boom predict, p3, m8, challenge 'touch'), a number said before the first or after the last (boom over-count feedback, robot 4 claps said 5, m3, challenge 'extra'), missing a quick one (boom under-count feedback, robot fast case, m6, challenge 'miss'), a big or loud one counting as more than one (robot big clap, m4, robot predict), judging 'more' by loudness or size (loud predict, giant vs mouse pair, p4, m2, challenge 'loud' and 'big'), and not stopping on the number when making actions (frog too-many feedback, p5, challenge 'stop').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagactcount is about counting events that vanish: the drum booms leave no mark and the child must answer after the sound stops; the frog has no counter, so the child counts aloud and presses Stop; the compare scene plays loud vs quiet and slow big vs quick small sounds; the bell waits for one finger per ring and then asks once the sound is gone. No other lab counts transient events; flagcount, flagoto and flagobj20 count objects that stay on screen, and flagbeat (English) finds the steady beat in a song rather than counting. The lab_distinct gate measures it under 30% against every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers the rules by doing: a wrong drum answer replays the round with feedback on too many or too few, pressing Stop early or late shows numbered arcs for every jump made in red, the loud/quiet pair is replayed until the child sees 3 and 3 match, and the bell scene shows the sound has gone but the raised fingers still hold the count. Done messages state each rule only after the task is complete.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'No, only things I can touch' (the child then counts 3 and 5 booms), 'The loud bangs' are more (3 loud and 3 quiet are confirmed the same), 'No, the sound has gone' (the five fingers keep the count after the bell stops), and 'Yes, big counts as 2' (the robot's big-clap count is a slip with its own fix).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions, each wrong option tagged with its slip and a message naming it: extra ('Do not say a number before the first one, or after the last one'), miss, touch, loud/quiet, big ('A big stamp is still one stamp'), same and stop. In the lab, wrong answers also name the slip: more booms than the drum made, a missed boom, too many or too few jumps with the target word, loud does not mean more, big stamps are not worth more, a finger without a ring.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use words like count, clap, jump, boom, finger and stop in short sentences of up to about 12 words; the adult text names the curriculum line and the slips plainly; validate_lessons readability passes for both. Canvas banners stay short, e.g. 'How many booms? Tap the number' and 'Ding! Put up one finger'.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid sentence is a rule, an example or a tip (one number for each, stop when it stops, loud and quiet are one each, fingers keep track, stop on the number); adult paragraphs give placement and key words, why sounds are harder than objects and how to scaffold, the common mistakes, and what each lab scene does. The content gate finds no filler phrases.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots in light and dark for every scene, including the ask states: the six number tiles are about 50 px wide with 20 px numerals, the three compare tiles (Loud more, Same, Quiet more) shrink their text to fit, the Stop tile is 216 px wide, banners fit on one line, and the robot's numbers sit clearly under each clap. Every action also has a large button under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: Play the drum, number keys 1-6 ('3 booms'), Jump and Stop, Play both drums with Loud more / Same / Quiet more, Start the bell and Put up a finger with ring keys, Right and Slip. Each boom, tap and ding is announced through the live region so a child who cannot see the flash can still count; the canvas aria-label follows every message, and the walk gate's axe run is clean in both themes.

sources: DfE (2021) Development Matters: non-statutory curriculum guidance for the EYFS, Mathematics, Reception: 'Count objects, actions and sounds'
Gelman, R. and Gallistel, C. R. (1978) The Child's Understanding of Number. Harvard University Press (the abstraction principle)
Fuson, K. C. (1988) Children's Counting and Concepts of Number. Springer (keeping track of counted items)
